name: Sarangkot
tagline: Pokhara's sunrise ridge and Nepal's busiest paragliding launch
meta_description: Sarangkot guide: sunrise over Dhaulagiri and Annapurna, tandem paragliding, the ZipFlyer zipline, how to get up from Lakeside and where to stay on the ridge.
summary: Sarangkot is a ridge-top village at about 1,600 m directly above Phewa Lake, 30–45 minutes by road from Lakeside. It is where Pokhara watches the sunrise over Dhaulagiri, Annapurna and Machhapuchhre, and where the paragliders and the ZipFlyer zipline take off. Go between October and March for clear mornings.
intro: Sarangkot rises about 800 m above Pokhara on the north side of Phewa Lake. Since 2015 it has been a ward of Pokhara city, but it still feels like a hill village: Brahmin, Chhetri and Magar houses, maize terraces, a few small temples and the ruins of an old hill fort, the kot that gives the place its name. The top of the ridge is around 1,600 m, high enough that a sweater is welcome at dawn even in October.

The reason everyone comes is the view. From the concrete viewing tower and the terraces around it, the Himalaya fills the northern skyline from Dhaulagiri (8,167 m) in the west, through the Annapurna massif and Machhapuchhre, to Lamjung Himal and, on the clearest days, Manaslu far to the east. Below to the south, Pokhara and the whole length of Phewa Lake spread out like a map. It is the widest mountain view you can reach by car from Pokhara.

Sarangkot is also one of the most popular paragliding sites in Asia. From late morning, dozens of tandem wings launch from the take-off field just below the summit and spiral down to the lakeshore. The ZipFlyer, a 1.8 km zipline, starts from the ridge and drops towards Hemja. Most visitors come for a pre-dawn sunrise outing and return to Lakeside for breakfast; a night in one of the ridge-top lodges gives you the sunrise without the 4:45 am alarm.
facts: ≈ 12 km · 30–45 min by car, then 10–15 min climb
Sunrise over Dhaulagiri and Annapurna, tandem paragliding, ZipFlyer

highlights.title: Sunrise over the Annapurnas
highlights.text: Arrive by about 5:45 am in winter and 5:15 am in October. The first light turns Machhapuchhre and Annapurna South pink while the valley is still dark, then moves west to Dhaulagiri. The show lasts about 20 minutes; stay for tea as the mist lifts off Phewa Lake.

highlights.title: Tandem paragliding launch
highlights.text: The take-off slope sits just below the summit at around 1,500–1,600 m. Watching a sky full of wings is a sight in itself even if you do not fly, and a 20–30 minute tandem flight lands on the lakeshore at Lakeside.

highlights.title: ZipFlyer down to Hemja
highlights.text: The ZipFlyer runs about 1.8 km from Sarangkot with a vertical drop of roughly 600 m, reaching speeds well over 100 km/h. The ride is over in under two minutes and ends at the ground station in the Seti valley near Hemja.

highlights.title: Sarangkot hill fort remains
highlights.text: A short walk west of the viewing tower brings you to the remains of the old kot, a hill fort used in the 18th century. Not much stands today, but it is quieter than the main terrace and gives an open view along the ridge.

highlights.title: Walk down to Lakeside
highlights.text: A stone trail drops from Sarangkot to the north end of Lakeside in about 1.5–2 hours, passing through village fields and forest. It is a good way to stretch your legs after sunrise and see rural life minutes from the town.

highlights.title: Overnight on the ridge
highlights.text: Simple lodges and a few mid-range hotels sit along the ridge. Staying overnight means a sunset over Phewa and Dhaulagiri, a quiet evening above the town lights and a five-minute walk to the sunrise point instead of an early drive.

how_to_reach.text: A paved road climbs from Lakeside via Bindhyabasini and the Sarangkot road to a parking area below the summit, about 12 km and 30–45 minutes by taxi. A sunrise taxi with waiting time costs roughly NPR 1,500–2,500. From the car park it is a 10–15 minute climb up steps to the viewing tower; a ticket of about NPR 50–100 is charged.

Fit walkers can hike up from the north end of Lakeside (Khapaudi) in about 2–2.5 hours, gaining about 800 m on a stone and dirt trail. An easier route starts from the Pokhara–Baglung road near Miruwa and takes about 1.5 hours. Start in the dark with a torch for sunrise, or walk up in the afternoon and sleep on the ridge.

where_to_stay: Most travellers sleep in Pokhara and visit Sarangkot at dawn, so our packages base you at Lakeside or Damside in hotels such as Hotel Barahi or Temple Tree Resort & Spa and drive up before sunrise. If you want to sleep on the ridge, there are several simple lodges and a few mid-range hotels along the road below the viewing tower, many with east-facing rooms. Standards are basic to moderate, hot water can be erratic and nights are cold from December to February, so bring a warm layer. We arrange a ridge-top room on request, depending on availability.
tips: Check the sky at 4:30 am before leaving Lakeside; if stars are out, the sunrise will almost certainly be clear.
Carry a down jacket or fleece for dawn, when it can be 0–5 °C on the ridge in December and January.
Weekends in October and November bring large crowds to the tower, so stand on the lower terraces for elbow room.
Book paragliding for the morning after your sunrise outing rather than the same day if you want both at their best.
Bring small notes in Nepali rupees for the entry ticket, tea and parking.

experiences.title: Sarangkot sunrise over Dhaulagiri and Annapurna
experiences.price_hint: ≈ NPR 1,500–2,500 per car, plus small entry fee
experiences.summary: The classic Pokhara morning: a pre-dawn drive up to the ridge at about 1,600 m and 20 minutes of first light moving across Machhapuchhre, Annapurna and Dhaulagiri. Back at Lakeside for breakfast by 8 am. Included in all our Pokhara tour packages.
body: Your driver collects you from the hotel at about 4:45–5:15 am depending on the month. The road winds up through Bindhyabasini and the Sarangkot villages, and in 30–45 minutes you reach the car park below the summit. A flight of steps leads to the main viewing tower and a series of terraces where tea stalls are already lit. In winter the sky in the east turns orange around 6:15; in October it is closer to 5:45.

The peaks catch light from east to west. Manaslu and Lamjung Himal glow first on clear days, then Annapurna II, Machhapuchhre with its split summit, Annapurna South and Hiunchuli, and finally Dhaulagiri far to the west. Below you, mist often lies on Phewa Lake and the town, burning off as the sun climbs. Photographers want a 70–200 mm lens for the peaks and a wide lens for the lake. Phone cameras work well too.

The best months are October to February, when the air is dry and views are clear on most mornings. In March and April haze from crop burning and dust can soften the view, and from June to September the mountains are hidden more often than not. If the morning is cloudy, wait half an hour; breaks in the cloud are common. Most people head down by 7:30 am, stopping at Bindhyabasini temple on the way.

faqs.q: What time should I leave for Sarangkot sunrise?
faqs.a: Leave Lakeside about 75 minutes before sunrise. That means roughly 4:45 am in October, 5:15 am in December and January and 4:45 am again by late March. The drive is 30–45 minutes and the climb from the car park another 10–15 minutes, and you want to be at the top before the sky starts to colour.

faqs.q: Which mountains can you see from Sarangkot?
faqs.a: On a clear morning you see Dhaulagiri (8,167 m) to the west, then Annapurna South, Hiunchuli, Annapurna I behind them, Machhapuchhre (6,993 m), Annapurna III, Annapurna IV, Annapurna II and Lamjung Himal. On exceptionally clear days Manaslu (8,163 m) appears far to the east. Everest is not visible from Sarangkot.

faqs.q: Can elderly people do the Sarangkot sunrise?
faqs.a: Yes. The car reaches a parking area close to the top, and the remaining climb is about 10–15 minutes of steps with rest points. Some viewing terraces are reachable with fewer steps. Bring a warm jacket because it is cold before dawn, and walk slowly in the dark. Those who cannot manage steps can still see the view from the road below.

experiences.title: Tandem paragliding from Sarangkot
experiences.summary: Run a few steps off the Sarangkot slope with a licensed pilot strapped behind you and glide 20–30 minutes over Phewa Lake with the Annapurnas behind. No experience needed. Pokhara is one of the most popular tandem paragliding sites in the world.
body: The operator picks you up at Lakeside and drives about 40 minutes to the take-off field just below the top of Sarangkot. The pilot fits you into a seat harness, explains the three things you need to do (walk, then run, then sit back) and waits for a steady breeze up the slope. Take-off is gentle: a few running steps and the wing lifts you off the grass. Flights launch from about 9:30 am to 3 pm, with the busiest window around midday when thermals are reliable.

The standard flight lasts 20–30 minutes. You circle in thermals above the ridge, often alongside Himalayan griffon vultures and black kites, then glide out over the lake with Machhapuchhre behind your shoulder. Longer cross-country flights of about an hour go further along the ridge. Landing is in a field on the lakeshore at the north end of Lakeside, a few minutes' walk from most hotels. If you feel well, ask the pilot for a few spirals before landing; if not, say so and the flight stays smooth.

Most operators take passengers between about 25 and 90 kg; some can take heavier passengers with a larger wing. Children are usually accepted from around 6 years with a parent's consent. Flights are cancelled in rain, strong wind or low cloud, and the season pauses or is reduced from mid-June to August. A GoPro photo and video package costs about US$ 15–25 extra. Tell your pilot if you are prone to motion sickness.

faqs.q: How much does paragliding in Pokhara cost?
faqs.a: A 20–30 minute tandem flight costs roughly US$ 70–90 for foreigners and about ₹6,500–8,500 or NPR 10,000–13,000 for Indian and Nepali visitors, including transport to Sarangkot and insurance. Photo and video add about US$ 15–25. A one-hour cross-country flight costs US$ 120–150. Prices rise in October and November, so book a day ahead in peak season.

faqs.q: What is the weight limit for paragliding in Pokhara?
faqs.a: Most Pokhara operators fly passengers from about 25 kg up to 90 kg. Some will take passengers up to about 100–110 kg with a larger tandem wing and an experienced pilot, sometimes with a surcharge. Tell the operator your exact weight when booking. Very light children may need a calm-air slot.

Tandem flights are flown by licensed pilots under rules set by Nepal's Civil Aviation Authority, and Pokhara has thousands of flights each season. Accidents are rare but do happen, so choose an established operator, check that insurance is included and do not fly if you are pregnant, have heart problems or recent back injuries. Flights are cancelled in poor weather.

experiences.title: ZipFlyer zipline from Sarangkot to Hemja
experiences.best_time: Morning, all year except heavy monsoon days
experiences.summary: One of the longest and steepest ziplines in the world: about 1.8 km with a vertical drop of roughly 600 m, reaching speeds of 120–140 km/h. You fly from the Sarangkot ridge to the Seti valley near Hemja in under two minutes. No fitness needed beyond climbing into a harness.
body: The ZipFlyer is run by HighGround Adventures, the same company that operates the Pokhara bungee tower. The launch station is on the Sarangkot ridge, a drive of about 40 minutes from Lakeside. After weighing in and signing a waiver, you are fitted into a seat harness and clipped to a trolley on a steel cable. Two riders can go on parallel lines at the same time, which is popular with couples and friends.

When the gate opens, gravity does the rest. The cable drops at an angle of up to about 56 degrees, and within seconds you are travelling at more than 100 km/h with the Seti valley rushing up and Machhapuchhre straight ahead. The ride lasts around a minute and a half. A braking system slows you smoothly at the ground station near Hemja, where staff unclip you and drive you back to Lakeside.

Riders generally need to weigh between about 35 and 125 kg; children who meet the minimum weight can ride. People with heart conditions, high blood pressure, back or neck problems and pregnant women should not ride. The line runs most of the year, but rides are paused in storms and heavy rain. A combined package with the 70 m bungee at Hemja or with paragliding is available. Book the day before in peak season.

faqs.q: How much does the Pokhara zipline cost?
faqs.a: The ZipFlyer costs roughly US$ 65–75 for foreigners, with a lower rupee rate for Indian and Nepali visitors, usually including return transport from Lakeside. Photo and video packages cost extra, and combo deals with the 70 m bungee jump at Hemja bring the per-activity price down. Check the current tariff before you travel, as rates are revised.

faqs.q: What is the minimum age or weight for the ZipFlyer?
faqs.a: The operator sets the limits by weight rather than age: roughly 35 kg minimum and 125 kg maximum per rider. Children who meet the weight can ride, usually with parental consent. Riders should not have heart conditions, high blood pressure, back or neck injuries, or be pregnant. Confirm the current limits when you book.

faqs.q: Is the ZipFlyer scarier than paragliding?
faqs.a: It is more intense but much shorter. The zipline is a fast, steep drop of about 90 seconds at up to 140 km/h, while paragliding is a slow, floating 20–30 minute flight. People who fear heights often find the zipline easier because it is over quickly and you never control anything; others find the speed the scary part.

faqs.q: How far is Sarangkot from Pokhara Lakeside?
faqs.a: Sarangkot is about 12 km by road from central Lakeside, a 30–45 minute drive on a paved road that winds up via Bindhyabasini. From the car park, the main viewing tower is a 10–15 minute climb by steps. On foot, the trail from the north end of Lakeside takes about 2–2.5 hours uphill.

faqs.q: Is the Sarangkot sunrise worth it?
faqs.a: On a clear morning, yes. You see Dhaulagiri, the Annapurna range and Machhapuchhre catch first light in turn, with Phewa Lake and Pokhara below. It is the best panorama you can reach by car in the Pokhara area. From June to August it is often cloudy, so the outing is more of a gamble then.

faqs.q: What is the entry fee for Sarangkot viewpoint?
faqs.a: A small fee of roughly NPR 50–100 per person is collected at the viewing tower area, with foreigners sometimes charged slightly more than Nepali citizens. Parking may be charged separately. Fees are set locally and can change, so carry small notes in Nepali rupees and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I stay overnight in Sarangkot?
faqs.a: Yes. There are several simple lodges and a few mid-range hotels along the ridge near the viewpoint. Staying gives you sunset over Phewa and Dhaulagiri, a quiet evening and a short walk to the sunrise point. Rooms are simpler than in Lakeside and it is cold at night from December to February.

faqs.q: Which is better for sunrise: Sarangkot or Australian Camp?
faqs.a: Sarangkot is easier: a 40 minute drive and a short climb, with Pokhara and Phewa Lake in the view. Australian Camp, at about 2,060 m, is higher and closer to the mountains and much quieter, but you need to drive to Kande and walk about 1–1.5 hours, usually staying overnight. For a single morning, choose Sarangkot.

faqs.q: Is Sarangkot good for families with young children?
faqs.a: Yes for the sunrise. The drive is short, the walk from the car park is manageable for most children over four, and tea stalls sell hot drinks. Dress children warmly. Paragliding is usually allowed from about 6 years and the ZipFlyer goes by weight (about 35 kg minimum), so check limits before promising a ride.

faqs.q: When does paragliding happen at Sarangkot?
faqs.a: Tandem flights launch roughly between 9:30 am and 3 pm, after the sun has warmed the slope and created thermals. The main season runs from late September to May, with October, November, February and March best. From mid-June to August flights are reduced or suspended by rain and cloud.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide to visit Sarangkot?
faqs.a: No. The viewpoint is a simple taxi ride and short climb, and there are signs at the top. A driver who knows the timings is useful for sunrise. If you plan to hike up or down through the villages, a local guide helps on the unsigned junctions, especially in the dark.

faqs.q: What should I wear for Sarangkot sunrise?
faqs.a: Layers. Before dawn it can be 0–5 °C in December and January and around 10 °C in October and March, warming quickly once the sun is up. Wear a warm jacket, a hat, and shoes with grip for the stone steps, and carry a small torch or phone light for the walk from the car park.
